paragraphs: Capsule neural networks assemble representations from child capsules into parent capsules. Earlier approaches often make these assignments through repeated clustering steps, creating substantial computational work. This paper changes the capsule structure so that the assignment can happen through learned matching, addressing the cost of routing while retaining the idea of building larger representations from smaller ones.

Each capsule contains adjustable receptors, and each child representation has a transmitter. A child sends its representation to parents whose receptors match its transmitter well. The authors also introduce a receptor skeleton that coordinates receptors across layers. It gives each receptor an assigned share of the overall objective, organizing the network into a hierarchical clustering process.

Experiments support both efficient clustering and better performance than capsule networks using earlier routing algorithms. The reported improvements cover image classification, generalization to affine transformations, recognition of overlapping objects, and separation of semantic information within representations. Together, these findings suggest that coordinating learned routing components can improve both computational efficiency and the representations produced by capsule networks.
icml-2021-a-receptor-skeleton-for-capsul.tldr: Learned receptors and a coordinating skeleton replace costly iterative capsule routing and improve results across several visual tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks become expensive as both their models and input graphs grow. Removing model weights alone leaves a major source of cost intact: the graph’s size and connectivity. This paper introduces unified GNN sparsification, which removes graph connections and model weights together to accelerate inference.

The framework also extends the lottery ticket idea to graph learning. A graph lottery ticket consists of a core portion of the graph data paired with a sparse neural network. Repeated sparsification identifies this pair from the full graph and model. The authors report that these tickets can be trained separately to match full training performance, starting from either random initialization or self-supervised pretraining.

Experiments span different architectures, node classification, and link prediction on small and large graph datasets. For node classification, reported multiply-accumulate savings range from 20% to 98% on small graphs and 25% to 85% on large graphs, with matching accuracy. Link prediction also shows substantial savings without reduced predictive performance. These results support treating graph structure and model parameters as a joint compression problem.
icml-2021-a-unified-lottery-ticket-hypot.tldr: Jointly pruning graph connections and neural-network weights identifies smaller graph models that match full-model performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Distributed training must balance communication costs against progress toward a solution. Gossip SGD reduces communication by having each worker average only with its neighbors. On large, sparsely connected networks, however, information spreads slowly, and the extra iterations needed for convergence can offset the communication savings.

Gossip-PGA adds occasional averaging across all workers to these local exchanges. Its key control is the period H between global averages. The analysis focuses on the transient stage before training reaches the regime of asymptotic linear speedup. For nonconvex problems, the stated transient-stage expression changes from Ω(β⁴n³/(1−β)⁴) to Ω(β⁴n³H⁴), where 1−β measures network connectivity.

This change makes the influence of network topology controllable through the averaging schedule. The paper also reports a better transient-stage complexity than local SGD, whose stated order is Ω(n³H⁴). Experiments using ResNet50 for image classification and BERT for language modeling support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a way to retain neighborhood communication while periodically correcting the slow coordination caused by sparse networks.
icml-2021-accelerating-gossip-sgd-with-p.tldr: Occasional global averaging accelerates Gossip SGD and makes its sensitivity to sparse network connectivity controllable through the averaging period.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires storing intermediate activations for backpropagation, putting pressure on limited device memory. ActNN addresses this storage requirement by keeping randomly quantized versions of activations. The central idea is to reduce the memory devoted to these intermediate values while accounting for how compression affects learning.

The authors prove convergence for general network architectures and derive an exact expression describing the gradient variance introduced by quantization. They use this analysis to design mixed-precision strategies that account for differences across feature dimensions, examples, and layers. This means the compression scheme can respond to activation heterogeneity instead of assigning every stored value the same precision.

Across the evaluated vision models for classification, detection, and segmentation, ActNN stores activations at an average of two bits with negligible accuracy loss. It reduces activation memory by a factor of 12 and enables batch sizes 6.6 to 14 times larger. The framework can be incorporated into dynamic graph systems such as PyTorch by replacing layers, connecting the theoretical analysis to a practical training modification.
icml-2021-actnn-reducing-training-memory.tldr: ActNN compresses stored training activations to two bits on average, substantially reducing memory use with negligible accuracy loss in the evaluated vision tasks.

paragraphs: A symmetric matrix’s cumulative empirical spectral measure describes the fraction of its eigenvalues below any chosen threshold. Approximating this distribution is useful because it also supports computing sums of functions of eigenvalues. This paper analyzes the accuracy of stochastic Lanczos quadrature, a randomized method for estimating that spectral distribution.

The main guarantee connects computation to a requested error level and confidence. Using independent vectors sampled uniformly from the unit sphere, the method achieves Wasserstein error at most t times the matrix’s spectral range with probability at least 1−η. The theorem specifies both the number of Lanczos iterations per vector and the number of sampled vectors needed, making the relationship between effort and accuracy explicit.

The authors also provide error bounds that can be evaluated after computation and depend on the particular matrix. These cover both Wasserstein distance and Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance, giving two ways to assess disagreement with the true spectral distribution. Numerical experiments demonstrate the quality of the bounds, supporting their use in understanding the reliability of spectral approximations.
icml-2021-analysis-of-stochastic-lanczos.tldr: The paper establishes probabilistic and matrix-dependent error bounds for approximating eigenvalue distributions with stochastic Lanczos quadrature.

paragraphs: Transfer learning adapts an existing model to a new task, often by freezing early layers and updating later ones. This reduces the need for data and computation. The paper identifies a problem with judging this process only by predictive accuracy: adaptation can improve target-domain accuracy while weakening the adversarial robustness inherited from the pretrained model.

CARTL coordinates pretraining and fine-tuning to address that loss. During pretraining, it uses feature distance minimization. During adaptation, it applies non-expansive fine-tuning to the target task. The two stages are designed together, making preservation of robustness part of the transfer procedure rather than relying on ordinary fine-tuning to retain it.

In the reported experiments, CARTL improves inherited robustness by up to about 28% compared with a baseline at the same degree of accuracy. This is a best reported improvement, not a uniform gain across every setting. The authors also investigate batch normalization and find that freezing those layers can further improve robustness transfer, highlighting their role in preserving properties learned before adaptation.
icml-2021-cartl-cooperative-adversariall.tldr: CARTL coordinates pretraining and fine-tuning to preserve adversarial robustness while maintaining target-task accuracy.

paragraphs: Neural decoders extend belief propagation by treating its decoding graph as a trainable neural network. This paper specializes that approach to cyclic codes, whose structure is preserved by cyclic shifts. The central proposal is to encode this symmetry directly into the decoder’s weights so that the learned computation respects a property already present in the code.

The resulting decoder is cyclically equivariant: shifting the input around the cycle produces the corresponding shift in its output. This gives a precise relationship between how related inputs are processed. Simulations on BCH codes and punctured Reed–Muller codes show that the proposed decoder consistently outperforms previous neural decoders for the cyclic codes evaluated.

The authors additionally introduce a list decoding procedure that substantially reduces decoding error probability on these code families. For certain high-rate codes, its performance is within 0.1 dB of maximum-likelihood decoding. That close comparison is specific to the stated codes. Together, the results support combining code-aware neural architecture with a stronger decoding procedure.
icml-2021-cyclically-equivariant-neural-.tldr: A neural decoder that respects cyclic shifts improves decoding results, with an additional list procedure approaching maximum-likelihood performance for certain high-rate codes.

paragraphs: The paper studies time series generated by an underlying symplectic evolution map, including flows of Hamiltonian systems that need not be separable. Many approaches first learn a continuous-time vector field or the Hamiltonian producing it. Here, the authors directly learn the map that advances the system between discrete time steps, without requiring a vector field to exist.

Their generating-function neural network, GFNN, approximates a generating function from which the evolution map is represented. This construction keeps the learned map exactly symplectic. Exactness refers to preservation of that geometric structure, rather than perfect prediction of every future state. The structure gives the authors a way to control how prediction errors accumulate.

Under the assumptions of their analysis, global prediction error grows at most linearly with long prediction time, improving on otherwise exponential growth. Direct map learning also avoids errors from estimating a vector field using finite differences and from numerically integrating that field. Numerical experiments support the claims, connecting the structural design to improved long-term prediction behavior.
icml-2021-data-driven-prediction-of-gene.tldr: GFNN learns exactly symplectic discrete evolution maps and, under stated assumptions, limits long-term prediction-error growth to a linear rate.

paragraphs: Conformal predictors wrap machine-learning models to provide error guarantees under weak assumptions about the data distribution. Their usefulness spans classification, regression, and anomaly detection, but their computational demands can make large datasets difficult to handle. This paper asks how much of that work can be reduced by exploiting the underlying prediction method.

The approach uses incremental and decremental learning: updating computations when data are added or removed. Rather than treating conformal prediction as a separate layer whose costs are fixed, the authors study it together with methods such as nearest neighbors, kernel density estimation, and kernel least-squares support vector machines. For these methods, they report an order-of-magnitude reduction in running time while retaining exact solutions.

Related ideas yield a linear speedup for the more difficult bootstrapping case. The paper also extends the techniques to improve an existing optimization for nearest-neighbor conformal regression. Empirical evaluation supports the findings, and the authors discuss which underlying methods suit this optimization strategy. The contribution is computational acceleration that preserves the computed conformal solutions.
icml-2021-exact-optimization-of-conforma.tldr: Incremental and decremental updates substantially accelerate conformal prediction for several underlying models while preserving exact solutions.

paragraphs: The stochastic shortest-path problem asks a learner to reach a destination when actions have uncertain outcomes. This paper studies a demanding version in which transition behavior is unknown and costs can be adversarial. It considers both full-information feedback and bandit feedback, where the learner has more restricted observations of costs.

The proposed algorithms achieve regret bounds of O(√(S²ADT⋆K)) with full information and O(√(S³A²DT⋆K)) with bandit feedback. Here S and A count states and actions, K counts episodes, D is the diameter, and T⋆ is the optimal policy’s expected hitting time. The square-root dependence on episodes means these bounds grow more slowly than the number of episodes, for fixed other quantities.

The full-information result improves the prior bound identified in the abstract, while the work also extends guarantees beyond known transitions. It introduces the combination of bandit feedback, adversarial costs, and unknown transitions. A gap remains between the general upper and cited lower bounds; for the special case of a stochastically oblivious adversary, the authors provide near-optimal regret algorithms.
icml-2021-finding-the-stochastic-shortes.tldr: New algorithms bound regret for stochastic shortest paths with unknown transitions and adversarial costs, including the bandit-feedback setting.

paragraphs: Contrastive pretraining can treat other data points as dissimilar even when they share semantic meaning with the current point. Weighting pairs through positive-unlabeled learning can make the objective unbiased and the learning procedure consistent. The authors argue that this still leaves an undesirable effect: semantically similar pairs can continue to be pushed apart, potentially affecting downstream tasks.

Large-margin contrastive learning addresses this behavior with a distance polarization regularizer, motivated by patterns in pairwise distances from metric learning. The method distinguishes pairs within a cluster from pairs across clusters. It then applies separation only to the latter, explicitly changing which relationships the representation learning process pushes apart.

The paper proves a tighter error bound for the proposed method and reports empirical advantages in image classification, sentence representation, and reinforcement learning. These findings provide both theoretical and experimental support for the approach. The central distinction is between correcting the aggregate training objective and controlling the treatment of individual pairs: the paper argues that the second remains important even after the first is addressed.
icml-2021-large-margin-contrastive-learn.tldr: Large-margin contrastive learning separates pairs across clusters while avoiding repulsion within clusters, with a tighter error bound and gains across several domains.

paragraphs: This paper develops a deep-learning framework for finding Markovian Nash equilibria in stochastic games with many agents. Such equilibria concern strategies based on the current state, with each agent responding to the others. The framework uses fictitious play and aims to make equilibrium computation more sample efficient and scalable.

Its design draws on theoretical analysis of forward-backward stochastic differential equations and their implementation with neural networks. The authors identify this connection as the source of improved sample efficiency. For symmetric games, they further exploit permutation invariance: the computation can respect the fact that exchanging agent identities does not change the game’s structure. This improves scalability and performance.

On an interbank lending and borrowing problem, the framework outperforms the compared deep fictitious play method across multiple metrics. It also handles simulations with 3,000 agents, which the authors describe as a new scale to their knowledge. A belief-space autonomous racing example demonstrates applicability in robotics. These results establish performance on the presented applications, including a large simulated multi-agent setting.
icml-2021-large-scale-multi-agent-deep-f.tldr: A deep fictitious-play framework improves sample efficiency and exploits game symmetry to compute equilibria in simulations with up to 3,000 agents.

paragraphs: A random utility model describes uncertainty over rankings of a collection of items. To select a winner from any offered subset, it samples a ranking and chooses the highest-ranked available item. The model therefore defines choice probabilities for every subset, linking a distribution over complete preferences to observable decisions among available options.

This paper asks how compactly those choice probabilities can be represented when approximation is allowed. The target is lossy compression of the model’s winning probabilities across all subsets. For a universe of n items, the authors prove that roughly n² bits suffice, up to the factors suppressed by their notation. They also prove optimality of this bound.

This is an exponential improvement over the standard representation. Along the way, the authors sharpen an earlier existence result concerning mixtures of multinomial logit models. They show that the required mixture size for approximating a general random utility model has order n, again up to suppressed factors. The contribution characterizes both the achievable compression and the representation size needed for this alternative family.
icml-2021-light-rums-51ad1a8064.tldr: Random utility models admit an optimal approximately quadratic-bit representation of choice probabilities, exponentially smaller than their standard representation.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects a small set of starting nodes to spread influence widely through a network. Standard formulations assume the network and its diffusion parameters are available. This paper instead starts with an unknown network and passively observed cascades that record which nodes became active at each step.

The authors develop algorithms with constant-factor approximation guarantees under mild conditions on the distribution of initial seed sets. They also introduce a network inference method for learning structure and diffusion parameters from cascade data. Compared with prior solutions, this method requires weaker assumptions and avoids maximum-likelihood estimation and convex programming.

A central result is that useful influence optimization remains possible even when diffusion parameters are difficult to learn. The algorithms strengthen the learn-then-optimize approach by retaining a constant approximation guarantee in that situation. They require no assumptions about network structure or diffusion parameters, while still relying on the stated conditions on seed distributions. This separates the information needed for effective seed selection from the potentially harder task of accurately recovering every diffusion parameter.
icml-2021-network-inference-and-influenc.tldr: Observed diffusion cascades can support constant-factor influence maximization under seed-distribution conditions, even when diffusion parameters are hard to learn.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning in games through passivity, a control-theory concept describing energy conservation and dissipation. Game dynamics form feedback systems, making this perspective useful for understanding how learning rules interact. The authors show that continuous-time Follow-the-Regularized-Leader dynamics, including replicator dynamics, are lossless: their associated energy is conserved rather than dissipated.

They also prove that passivity implies bounded regret, connecting a control-theory property to an online-learning performance guarantee. Motivated by the energy structure of FTRL, they construct a family of lossless learning dynamics with simple gradient-based energy functions. This family is closed under convex combinations, so convex combinations of FTRL dynamics are also lossless and have bounded regret.

The framework supports results about both global asymptotic stability and Poincaré recurrence. In particular, coupling a lossless learning rule with a lossless game can preserve energy in the combined system and produce recurrent, pendulum-like behavior. The result helps explain why strong regret properties can coexist with repeated motion through strategy space in the game settings covered by the analysis.
icml-2021-online-optimization-in-games-v.tldr: A control-theory analysis links passive learning dynamics to bounded regret and explains recurrent behavior when lossless learners interact with lossless games.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to learn successive tasks while retaining what it learned earlier. Catastrophic forgetting occurs when this retention fails. The paper proposes adding generative regularization to a Bayesian inference framework, with the aim of enriching the features learned during each task and improving their usefulness across the learning sequence.

The construction uses energy-based models and Langevin dynamic sampling to form a generative regularization term for classification models. Training combines this term with the discriminative loss used for classification. The resulting objective asks the model to satisfy both kinds of learning signal, making the generative component part of how its representations are shaped.

Experiments across a variety of tasks show better results than the state-of-the-art methods compared in the paper and support the approach’s ability to avoid catastrophic forgetting in those evaluations. The abstract reports improvements over baseline methods exceeding 15% on Fashion-MNIST and 10% on CUB. These empirical findings support generative regularization as a useful addition to Bayesian continual learning, without establishing that forgetting disappears in every possible task sequence.
icml-2021-overcoming-catastrophic-forget.tldr: Combining generative regularization with Bayesian continual learning reduces catastrophic forgetting and improves results across the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: The Legendre Memory Unit is a recurrent neural network with a linear time-invariant memory component. This paper uses that structure to build a simplified variant whose training can be parallelized. The model can still run recurrently during inference, so the computational organization used for training need not be the same as the one used to process inputs afterward.

The authors report training speedups of up to 200 times. They also describe the parallelization scheme as applicable to deep networks whose recurrent components are linear dynamical systems. This identifies the structural condition that makes the scheme useful beyond the particular LMU architecture studied.

Across seven benchmarks, the new architecture improves accuracy relative to the original LMU and a range of published LSTM and transformer networks. It establishes a reported state-of-the-art result on permuted sequential MNIST. On IMDB sentiment analysis, it outperforms the compared DistilBERT and LSTM models while using half the parameters. The findings show that the simplified architecture can combine faster training with strong predictive performance in the evaluated sequence tasks.
icml-2021-parallelizing-legendre-memory-.tldr: A simplified Legendre Memory Unit enables parallel training with reported speedups up to 200 times while retaining recurrent inference and improving benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries from an incomplete matrix. This paper studies that task with user-level privacy and develops a jointly differentially private version of alternating least squares. The goal is to preserve useful predictions while accounting for the noise introduced to protect users.

The authors provide the first global convergence analysis of alternating least squares with differential-privacy noise. Their method achieves nearly optimal sample complexity in terms of the numbers of users and items. Its error bounds also scale better with those quantities than the compared Private Frank–Wolfe method. These dependencies matter because the size of the user and item populations is central to practical matrix-completion problems.

On standard benchmarks, the algorithm combined with carefully designed sampling procedures is substantially more accurate than the existing techniques evaluated. The paper reports the best known privacy–utility trade-off both theoretically and empirically. These results motivate the authors’ description of the method as a promising practical private embedding model, while keeping that practical claim tied to the presented analysis and benchmark evidence.
icml-2021-private-alternating-least-squa.tldr: A private alternating least-squares method improves theoretical error scaling and benchmark accuracy for matrix completion with user-level privacy.

paragraphs: In a thresholding bandit problem, a learner samples uncertain options and identifies those whose mean outcomes exceed a specified threshold. This paper studies the probability of making at least one incorrect classification after a fixed sampling budget. Its analysis is problem dependent, focusing on the particular configuration of means rather than only a broad worst-case description.

The authors consider two forms of structure in the ordered sequence of arm means. In one, the means increase monotonically. In the other, they form a concave sequence. For each setting, they develop algorithms and nearly matching upper and lower bounds on error probability. The upper bounds describe achievable performance, while the lower bounds characterize the difficulty that algorithms must face.

A notable finding is that the optimal error bounds in both structured settings have the same order as those for a two-arm problem. This shows how strongly shape information can change the statistical difficulty of identifying above-threshold arms. The conclusion concerns the stated error-probability bounds under monotonicity or concavity and a fixed budget.
icml-2021-problem-dependent-view-on-stru.tldr: Under monotone or concave arm means, thresholding bandits admit nearly matching error bounds of the same order as a two-arm problem.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation regression transfers a numerical predictor from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. The paper investigates why aligning deep representations has been less successful for regression. Its central finding is that regression is sensitive to feature scaling, and distribution alignment can alter that scale in ways that impede transfer.

The proposed method compares representation spaces through orthogonal bases, avoiding dependence on feature scale. Drawing on the geometry of the Grassmann manifold, the authors define a distance between representation subspaces and minimize it during learning. This targets a geometric relationship between domains rather than directly forcing their full representation distributions to match.

The method also includes a basis-mismatch penalty that aligns the ordering of orthogonal bases across the two spaces while preserving the intended geometry. Evaluation covers three domain-adaptation regression benchmarks, two introduced by the paper. The authors report significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods compared. These findings provide early positive evidence for deep regression transfer through subspace alignment and identify feature scale as a consequential design consideration.
icml-2021-representation-subspace-distan.tldr: Aligning the geometry of representation subspaces improves domain-adaptation regression while avoiding the feature-scaling problem of distribution alignment.

paragraphs: Self-supervised text pretraining has helped translation when paired training data are scarce, but it often provides little additional benefit when such data are abundant. This paper addresses that resource-rich setting by training with self-supervised and supervised signals together. Its aim is to make the two sources of information complement each other during translation learning.

The proposed F2-XEnDec approach creates training examples through a crossover encoder-decoder process that combines monolingual and parallel sentences. The translation model learns from these interbred examples. This gives self-supervised information a direct role in the joint training procedure, rather than relying solely on a separate pretraining stage to benefit the supervised task.

Experiments on WMT’14 English–German and English–French show substantial improvements over several strong baselines. With back translation incorporated, the method reaches 46.19 BLEU on English–French, reported as a new state of the art. Results also show improved robustness to input perturbations, including code-switching noise. The reported benefits therefore include translation quality and resilience to the kinds of mixed-language inputs considered in the evaluation.
icml-2021-self-supervised-and-supervised.tldr: F2-XEnDec jointly trains on combined monolingual and parallel examples to improve resource-rich translation quality and robustness to input noise.

paragraphs: SPADE evaluates a model’s adversarial robustness through a black-box analysis of its inputs and outputs. It constructs graphs that approximate the corresponding data manifolds and studies a bijective distance mapping between them. The aim is to characterize how the model changes relationships among data points, connecting that geometry to sensitivity under perturbations.

Using the generalized Courant–Fischer theorem, the authors define a model-level SPADE score. Under the manifold setting, they prove that this score upper-bounds the best Lipschitz constant. This provides a theoretical connection between a quantity computed through spectral analysis and a measure of how strongly output changes can respond to input changes.

The method also uses dominant generalized eigenvectors to embed the graph and assign robustness scores to individual data points. These scores are intended to reveal especially vulnerable samples and can guide adversarial training. Experiments with neural networks trained on MNIST and CIFAR-10 produce promising results. The contribution therefore includes both a global robustness assessment and a way to identify where vulnerability is concentrated.
icml-2021-spade-a-spectral-method-for-bl.tldr: SPADE uses spectral analysis of input and output graphs to score model robustness and identify samples vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Predicting a spreadsheet formula requires understanding what the surrounding cells mean. Earlier approaches commonly used input-output examples that treated rows as separate cases. This paper argues that such a setup misses useful information: relationships across rows and columns, and headers that explain the meaning of the data.

SpreadsheetCoder predicts formulas from this broader tabular context. Its BERT-based architecture represents the surrounding table in both row-oriented and column-oriented forms, incorporating headers alongside cell contents. The model is trained on a large spreadsheet dataset. This design makes the table’s organization part of the evidence used to choose a formula.

The reported top-choice prediction accuracy is 42.51%, substantially above baselines that omit rich tabular context. In a Google Sheets comparison, SpreadsheetCoder assists 82% more users with composing formulas than the rule-based system. These findings measure different aspects of the approach: selecting the correct formula as the first prediction and reaching more users with useful assistance. Both support the value of learning from spreadsheet structure as well as individual cell values.
icml-2021-spreadsheetcoder-formula-predi.tldr: SpreadsheetCoder uses headers and row-and-column context to predict formulas, improving prediction accuracy and helping more Google Sheets users than the compared systems.

paragraphs: Regression models can have different prediction accuracy across demographic groups. This paper studies where those disparities come from and how an algorithm might reduce them while preserving predictive performance. It begins with a theoretical decomposition, giving a structured account of differences in group-level accuracy.

The decomposition connects accuracy disparity to two kinds of distributional distance: differences between marginal label distributions and differences between conditional representations. These distinguish variation in the target values across groups from variation in the representations considered conditionally. Motivated by this result, the authors design an algorithm that uses statistical distances to align distributions and reduce the resulting disparity.

The paper also analyzes the game-theoretic optima of its proposed objectives, linking the training formulation to a theoretical account of its solutions. Experiments on five benchmark datasets support the analysis: the results suggest that the algorithms can reduce accuracy disparity while maintaining the predictive power of the regression models. The contribution combines an explanation of the problem with an intervention whose empirical benefits include both disparity reduction and retained prediction quality.
icml-2021-understanding-and-mitigating-a.tldr: An error decomposition motivates distribution-alignment algorithms that reduce demographic accuracy disparities in regression while retaining predictive power in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Time-series models can benefit from information about how the shape of observed data changes over time. This paper combines that idea with graph convolutional networks. It uses topological descriptors to capture structural information that may complement the representations learned by a time-aware neural network.

The method introduces zigzag persistence into the network’s temporal processing. Zigzag persistence provides a mathematical framework for tracking important topological features as observations evolve. To make the resulting information usable by the model, the authors develop a summary called a zigzag persistence image. They also derive theoretical stability guarantees for this summary, giving a mathematical basis for its use as a representation.

The resulting Z-GCNET architecture includes a time-aware topological layer. Evaluation covers traffic forecasting and Ethereum blockchain price prediction across four time-series datasets. The reported results outperform 13 state-of-the-art comparison methods. These findings support the usefulness of time-conditioned topological information in the evaluated forecasting settings, while the stability analysis separately addresses a theoretical property of the proposed summary.
icml-2021-z-gcnets-time-zigzags-at-graph.tldr: Z-GCNET adds stable summaries of evolving topological structure to graph neural networks and improves forecasting across four evaluated datasets.
